geometry_edits.rationale: Replace the sealed cantilever with a split-wing organization to create a clearer dominant mass plus a void-driven threshold.
Orient the split so the public gap can read across the frontage rather than as a closed box.
Keep a minimal connector so the split remains one composition instead of fragmented parts.
Attach the mass to the ground with a readable base element to strengthen neighborhood public threshold behavior.
Keep the spine low so the upper mass still reads as the dominant program volume.
Make the base substantial enough to register as an active street edge without overpowering the void.

graph_edits.rationale: The current cantilever reads too box-like and sealed; split the dominant mass to create a clearer primary/support relationship and open a legible ground threshold.
Establish a ground-connected spine so the mass can read as neighborhood-living rather than a floating sealed block.
Keep the split volumes connected but make the connection secondary so the void remains legible.
Add a void operation to carve a public court that can answer the frontage and give the plan a real open-space figure.
Use a bounded courtyard margin that is large enough to read as usable public space, not a decorative notch.
Open the court toward the programmed access side to align the void with the public threshold.

rationale: The mass reads as a compact, mostly coherent object in all four views, so it avoids total fragmentation, but the form is still dominated by a generic blocky stacking/overhang rather than a clearly authored neighborhood-living gesture. The parcel is broadly contained, but the dominant silhouette does not strongly resolve the thin green boundary into a specific orientation or public-space figure. Most importantly, the verified road frontage/access edge is not answered by a legible court, notch, undercut, or active seam; the ground condition reads sealed and semantically passive. The apparent voids are too small/indistinct to count as public threshold space. The section is not wrong in a hard structural sense, but it lacks a convincing mixed-use ground-to-upper hierarchy and feels closer to an arbitrary compact object than a building with active neighborhood frontage.
